question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \] The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=5$ and $\lambda_2=10.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D=P^T \! A P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

Step 1. Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=5\quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=10$

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=5,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=10,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 10 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6 \end{bmatrix} - 10 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-10I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \\ \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -2 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-2.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-2.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-2.$ Computing $A-(-2)I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A + 2 I &= \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix} + 2 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 0\\ 2 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 - 2R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 2 & 0\\ 0& 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-2x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -2x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, setting $x_2=1,$ we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{5}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P\mathbin{:}$ \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\|\mathbf{v}_2\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{2\sqrt{5}}{5} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{5} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad D = \begin{bmatrix} 8 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 \end{bmatrix} \] Consider the matrices shown above. Given that $D=P^T \! AP,$ where $P$ is an orthogonal matrix, which of the following could be the second column of the matrix $P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

First, note that $A$ is symmetric and $D$ is diagonal. Therefore, $D=P^T \! AP$ gives an orthogonal diagonalization of $A.$

From the diagonal matrix $D$ we deduce that the eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are $\lambda_1=8$ and $\lambda_2=-5.$ So, the second column of $P$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-5.$

Now, we need to find an eigenvector that corresponds to $\lambda_2=-5.$ Computing $A-(-5)I,$ we get

\begin{align*} A + 5 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 6 \\ 6 & -1 \end{bmatrix} + 5 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*}

So, we have a system of linear equations with the augmented matrix $M$ which we reduce to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 9 & 6 & 0\\ 6 & 4 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 & := R_2 - \dfrac 2 3R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|c} 9 & 6 & 0\\ 0& 0 & 0 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

The reduced matrix above has one pivot column (the $1$st one). Thus, $x_2$ is a free variable. From the first equation, we obtain $x_1=-\dfrac 2 3x_2.$ Hence, the general solution is

\[ \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac 2 3x_2 \\ x_2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad x_2 \in \mathbb{R}. \]

Therefore, setting $x_2=-3,$ we get the eigenvector

\[ \mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}, \]

where $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{13}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm, we obtain the second column of $P\mathbin{:}$ \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2}{\|\mathbf{v}_2\|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{13}} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2\sqrt{13}}{13} \\ -\dfrac{3\sqrt{13}}{13} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \] The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=3$ and $\lambda_2=-1.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D=P^T \! A P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

Step 1. Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=3\quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-1$

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=3,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 3 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} - 3 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-3I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-1,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-1) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} + 1 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{2},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} & -\dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \\ \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} & \dfrac{\sqrt 2}{2} \end{bmatrix} \]

question.text: \[ A=\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} \] The matrix $A$ above has eigenvalues $\lambda_1=9$ and $\lambda_2=-8.$ Find a diagonal matrix $D$ and an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that $D=P^T \! A P.$
question.explanation:
Recall that a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if there exists an orthogonal matrix $P$ such that

\[ A=PDP^T, \] where $D$ is a diagonal matrix. Equivalently,

\[ D=P^TAP. \]

Moreover, a matrix $A$ is orthogonally diagonalizable if and only if it is symmetric.

Note that $A$ is symmetric. Therefore, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Let's now go through the process.

Step 1. Notice that we already have the eigenvalues of $A\mathbin{:}$

$\qquad$ $\lambda_1=9\quad$ and $\quad \lambda_2=-8$

Step 2. Now, we need to find an eigenvector basis of $A.$

  • For $\lambda_1=9,$ we have \begin{align*} A - 9 I &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} - 9 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & -4 \\ -4 & -16 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-8I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_1$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_1 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_1 }{\| \mathbf{v}_1 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} -4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

  • For $\lambda_2=-8,$ we have \begin{align*} A - (-8) I &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -4 \\ -4 & -7 \end{bmatrix} + 8 \begin{bmatrix} 1& 0\\ 0& 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 16 & -4 \\ -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-8)I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}$ gives the eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}.$ Dividing $\mathbf{v}_2$ by its norm $\| \mathbf{v}_2 \| = \sqrt{17},$ we get \[ \dfrac{\mathbf{v}_2 }{\| \mathbf{v}_2 \|} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix}. \]

Step 3. We construct the diagonal matrix $D$ and the orthogonal matrix $P$ in the usual way, and this gives us the following: \[ D = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & 0 \\ 0 & -8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad P = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} & \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} \\ \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{17}} & \dfrac{4}{\sqrt{17}} \end{bmatrix} \]
